type: time; also linking (a discourse marker: *Now, listen…*)
position: any position — usually end; front for contrast or as a discourse marker; mid in formal writing (*We now turn to…*)
modifies: verbs and clauses; also *just now*, *right now*, *by now*
contrast: Russian *сейчас* also means 'in a moment' (*сейчас приду*); English does not use *now* for that: *I'll be right there* or *I'm coming*, not *I come now*. *Now that…* (*Now that you're here, we can start*) is a conjunction and belongs to another dictionary. *Right now* is 'at this very moment' or 'immediately', never 'just a moment ago' — that is *just now*. With a length of time, *now* is Russian *уже*: *We've lived here ten years now* (*мы живём здесь уже десять лет*), not *already ten years*.

senses.gloss: At the present moment.
examples: I can't talk *now* — I'm driving.
She's in a meeting right *now*.
Where are you living *now*?

senses.gloss: At this period of time, in contrast with the past.
examples: I used to hate coffee, but *now* I drink three cups a day.
Most people *now* pay with their phones.
Prices are much higher *now* than when I was a kid.

senses.gloss: In the situation that exists after what has just happened; as a result.
examples: You missed the last bus — how are you getting home *now*?
She read the letter, so *now* she knows the truth.
We've come this far; we can't turn back *now*.

senses.gloss: Immediately; without any delay.
examples: Leave *now* or you'll miss the bus.
I need that report *now*, not tomorrow.
Call her right *now*, before she goes to bed.

senses.gloss: With a length of time: up to the present, counting from when something began.
examples: We've been married twenty years *now*.
It's been three weeks *now*, and she still hasn't called.
I've lived in Texas for a long time *now*.

senses.gloss: At the point in a past story being told; by that time.
examples: It was *now* completely dark, and we were lost.
The crowd was *now* chanting his name.

senses.gloss: Only a moment ago (*just now*).
examples: Your mom called *just now*.
Who was that at the door *just now*?

senses.gloss: Occasionally, from time to time (*now and then*, *now and again*).
examples: We still see each other every *now and then*.
*Now and again* he sends me a postcard.

senses.gloss: Used to get attention, move to a new point, or soften a warning or comfort.
examples: *Now*, let's look at the second question.
*Now*, *now*, don't cry — it's only a scratch.
*Now* listen to me carefully.

type: time; also linking (*in that case*, *but then*)
position: any position — 'next' front, after *and*, or mid (*she then left*); 'at that time' usually end; 'in that case' front or end
contrast: *then* is not *than*: *She's taller than me*, never *taller then me* — the two sound almost the same in fast speech and native speakers misspell them too. *then* is an adverb, not a conjunction, so careful writing joins two clauses with *and then*: *I finished my work, and then I went home*, not *I finished my work, then I went home*. The adjective use (*the then president*) belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: After that; next in time or in order.
examples: We had dinner, and *then* we went to a movie.
First add the flour, *then* the eggs.
Turn left at the light, and *then* it's the second house on the right.

senses.gloss: At that time, in the past or the future.
examples: We were living in Chicago *then*.
Call me Friday — I'll know more *then*.
Back *then*, nobody had a cell phone.

senses.gloss: In that case; so; as a result.
examples: If you're tired, *then* go to bed.
"I don't have a car." "*Then* how did you get here?"
Okay *then*, I'll see you tomorrow.

senses.gloss: In addition; on top of that (*and then*).
examples: The rent is high, and *then* there's parking to pay for.
I have to finish this report, and *then* there are all those emails.

senses.gloss: On the other hand; considering this (*but then*, *then again*).
examples: He's very quiet, but *then* his father was the same way.
I might go to the party. *Then again*, I might just stay home.

position: front or end — usually end
contrast: No preposition: *I'm working today*, not *on today*. Russian *сегодня утром / сегодня вечером* is *this morning / this evening* or *tonight* — never *today morning* or *today evening*. When *today* is the subject (*Today is Monday*) it is a noun and belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: On this day.
examples: I have a dentist appointment *today*.
What are you doing *today*?
The store closes early *today*.

senses.gloss: At the present period; nowadays.
examples: Kids *today* spend hours online.
*Today*, most homes in the US have internet access.
Few people *today* remember how to use a paper map.

position: front or end — usually end
contrast: No preposition: *See you tomorrow*, not *on tomorrow*. *Завтра утром* is usually *tomorrow morning* (*tomorrow in the morning* sounds clumsy); *послезавтра* is *the day after tomorrow*. A timetable takes the present simple: *The flight leaves at seven tomorrow*. As a subject (*Tomorrow is Friday*) it is a noun and belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: On the day after today.
examples: I'll call you *tomorrow*.
*Tomorrow* we're driving up to the lake.
The package should arrive *tomorrow* morning.

position: front or end — usually end
contrast: Past simple, not the present perfect: *I saw her yesterday*, not *I have seen her yesterday*. *Вчера вечером* is *yesterday evening* or *last night*; *вчера ночью* is *last night*, never *yesterday night*. *Позавчера* is *the day before yesterday*. As a subject (*Yesterday was cold*) it is a noun and belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: On the day before today.
examples: I ran into your sister *yesterday*.
It rained all day *yesterday*.
*Yesterday* afternoon we finally finished the project.

senses.gloss: Very recently, as it seems (*only yesterday*).
examples: It seems like only *yesterday* that we moved in.
I remember it as if it happened *yesterday*.

position: front or end — usually end
contrast: Russian splits *сегодня вечером* and *сегодня ночью*; English *tonight* covers both, from about sunset on. The night that has just ended is *last night*, not *tonight* or *this night*. No preposition: *Are you free tonight?*, not *at tonight*.

senses.gloss: On the evening or night of today.
examples: Are you free *tonight*?
It's supposed to snow *tonight*.
*Tonight* we're having pizza and watching a movie.

position: mid or end — end is most common; mid after an auxiliary (*will soon be*); front for a new stage in a story
contrast: *No sooner* fronted forces inversion and takes *than*, not *when*: *No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang*. *As soon as* takes the present for a future event: *Call me as soon as you arrive*, not *as soon as you will arrive*. *soon* is not *early*: *I got up early*, not *I got up soon*.

senses.gloss: In a short time from now or from the time mentioned.
examples: Dinner will be ready *soon*.
*Soon* after we arrived, it started to rain.
We'll *soon* find out who won.

senses.gloss: Early or quickly; before the time expected.
examples: How *soon* can you get here?
It's too *soon* to say whether the treatment is working.
The *sooner* we leave, the *sooner* we'll get there.

senses.gloss: Rather; preferably (*would sooner*, *would just as soon*).
examples: I'd *sooner* walk than wait an hour for the bus.
She would *sooner* quit than apologize to him.
I'd just as *soon* stay home tonight.

position: end — also front (*Later, …*) and mid (*she later became…*)
comparison: not gradable — it is already the comparative of *late* (*much later*, *a little later*)
modifies: verbs; follows a time phrase (*two years later*)
form: comparative of *late*, used as a time adverb in its own right
contrast: *two days later* counts forward from a past event (*спустя два дня*); counting forward from now is *in two days*: *I'll be back in two days*, not *two days later*. Standing alone, *later* or *afterward* is safe; *after* at the end (*I'll do it after*) is casual. Do not confuse with *latter* (the second of two).

senses.gloss: At some time after now; afterward.
examples: I'll call you *later*.
Can we talk about this *later*?
See you *later*!

senses.gloss: After the past time or event mentioned.
examples: Three years *later*, they got married.
She *later* became a federal judge.
*Later* that night, the power went out.

senses.gloss: At a time after the usual, expected or stated time.
examples: Can we meet *later* than six?
The kids stayed up *later* than usual.

position: mid or end — also front
contrast: The tense follows the meaning: one event 'not long ago' takes the past simple (*I recently bought a car*); a period 'lately' takes the present perfect (*I've been busy recently*). *lately* covers only the second meaning: *I recently met her*, not *I lately met her*.

senses.gloss: Not long ago.
examples: We *recently* moved to Austin.
The bridge was *recently* repainted.
*Most recently*, she ran a small bakery in Denver.

senses.gloss: During the period up to now.
examples: Have you seen any good movies *recently*?
I haven't been sleeping well *recently*.

position: mid or end — mid is neutral (*I've already seen it*); end adds emphasis or surprise
modifies: verbs and clauses; also time expressions (*already midnight*)
contrast: *already* goes in affirmative sentences; negatives and ordinary questions take *yet* (*Have you finished yet?*); *already* in a question shows surprise. The present perfect is standard, but American English freely uses the past simple: *I already ate*. Russian *уже не* is *not … anymore* or *no longer*: *He doesn't work here anymore*, not *He already doesn't work here*. *all ready* is two words meaning 'fully prepared': *We're all ready to go*.

senses.gloss: Before now or before a particular time, often sooner than expected (in a question, with surprise: so soon?).
examples: I've *already* eaten, thanks.
By the time we got there, the movie had *already* started.
You're leaving *already*?

senses.gloss: Informal American: used after a command or complaint to show impatience.
examples: Enough *already*! We get it.
Just make up your mind *already*.

type: time; also degree (*yet another*) and linking (*and yet*)
position: end — in negatives and questions; mid in *have yet to*, *may yet*; before its word in *yet another*, *yet again*
contrast: Russian *ещё* is both *yet* and *still*: *I haven't decided yet* (*ещё не решил*) but *I still live there* (*всё ещё живу*); *still* goes before a negative auxiliary (*He still hasn't called*), *yet* at the end (*He hasn't called yet*). In questions *yet* is Russian *уже*: *Has the mail come yet?* American English allows the past simple: *Did you eat yet?* *have yet to* looks affirmative but is negative. The conjunction *yet* (*simple yet effective*) belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: Up to now; so far (in negatives and questions, and after a superlative).
senses.ru: ещё (не); уже (в вопросах); на сегодняшний день
examples: I haven't finished *yet*.
"Are we there *yet*?" "Not *yet*."
That was her best album *yet*.

senses.gloss: Not so far, although it is expected (*have yet to*, *be yet to*).
examples: The winner has *yet* to be announced.
I have *yet* to meet anyone who actually likes that show.

senses.gloss: Still; even now; at some time in the future.
examples: We may *yet* win this game.
There's hope for him *yet*.
Don't give up — this plan could *yet* work.

senses.gloss: Even more; one more time (*yet another*, *yet again*, before a comparative).
examples: The flight was delayed *yet* again.
That's *yet* another reason to stay home.
We got *yet* more snow overnight.

senses.gloss: Nevertheless; in spite of that (*and yet*).
examples: It's a tiny town, and *yet* it has three bookstores.
He knew it was risky, and *yet* he went ahead anyway.

ru: всё ещё, до сих пор; всё же
type: time; also linking (*nevertheless*) and degree (*still better*)
position: mid — before the main verb, after *be*, before a negative auxiliary; front for 'nevertheless'
contrast: Before a negative auxiliary: *He still hasn't called* (*всё ещё не*), not *He hasn't still called*. *still* is for something continuing, *not yet* for something not started, *not anymore* for something that stopped. Russian *ещё один* is *another* or *one more*, not *still one*. The adjective 'not moving' (*still water*, and also *sit still*, *hold still*, *keep still*) belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: Continuing up to now or up to the time mentioned.
examples: She *still* lives with her parents.
Are you *still* at work?
It was midnight, and he *still* hadn't called.

senses.gloss: Nevertheless; even so.
examples: It rained all weekend. *Still*, we had a great time.
He drives me crazy, but he's *still* my brother.
The hotel was expensive, but it was *still* worth it.

senses.gloss: Even; to a greater degree (with comparatives and *another*, *more*).
examples: The next day was hotter *still*.
Ten minutes is good; five is *still* better.
Better *still*, call ahead and reserve a table.

position: end — also mid (*she immediately called*) and before its word (*immediately after*, *immediately below*)
modifies: verbs; prepositions and adverbs of time and place (*immediately after*)
contrast: British English also uses *immediately* as a conjunction (*Immediately I saw her, I knew*); American English says *as soon as* or *the moment*: *As soon as I saw her, I knew*.

senses.gloss: At once; without any delay.
examples: Please call 911 *immediately*.
She *immediately* recognized his voice.
The new rules take effect *immediately*.

senses.gloss: Directly next in time, place or relationship, with nothing between.
examples: We left *immediately* after the ceremony.
The restrooms are *immediately* to your left.
Only the people *immediately* affected were told.

position: mid or end — also front
contrast: False friend: *eventually* never means 'possibly, if need be' (*эвентуально*, German *eventuell*). It says the thing did or will happen in the end, usually after a delay: *He eventually agreed* = *в конце концов согласился*. For 'possibly' use *possibly* or *potentially*. Unlike *finally*, it cannot introduce the last point of a list.

senses.gloss: In the end, after a long time, a delay or a series of events.
examples: We waited two hours, and the bus *eventually* came.
You'll get used to the cold *eventually*.
*Eventually*, they sold the house and moved to Florida.

position: mid — front when it introduces the last point
contrast: *finally*, *at last* and *eventually* differ: *at last* stresses relief and cannot begin a last point in a list; *eventually* is neutral 'in the end' and also cannot list; *lastly* only lists. Mid position for 'after a long time' (*We finally got home*), front with a comma for the last point (*Finally, …*).

senses.gloss: After a long time, often with relief or impatience.
examples: We *finally* got home at two in the morning.
After six years, she *finally* finished her degree.
*Finally*! I thought you'd never get here.

senses.gloss: As the last in a series of points or actions.
examples: *Finally*, I'd like to thank my parents.
Mix the dry ingredients, add the eggs, and *finally* pour in the milk.

senses.gloss: In a way that settles something for good.
examples: The lawsuit was *finally* settled out of court.
Nothing has been *finally* decided yet.

position: end — also front (*Afterward, …*)
form: -ward — from *after*; *afterwards* is the British form, also common in the US
contrast: Russian *после* is both a preposition and an adverb; in English the adverb is *afterward* or *later*, while *after* normally needs an object: *We went for coffee afterward*, but *after the movie*. *afterward* never takes an object: *after dinner*, not *afterward dinner*.

senses.gloss: After the time or event mentioned; later.
examples: We saw a play and went out for dessert *afterward*.
Shortly *afterward*, the police arrived.
I felt terrible about it *afterward*.

position: end
contrast: Russian *заранее* is *beforehand*, *in advance* or *ahead of time*, not *before* alone: *Let me know beforehand*. *beforehand* never takes an object: *before the meeting*, not *beforehand the meeting*.

senses.gloss: Before a particular event; in advance.
examples: Let me know *beforehand* if you can't come.
We bought the tickets online *beforehand*.
I wish someone had warned me *beforehand*.

position: front or end
modifies: clauses, usually in the present simple
contrast: For a general situation compared with the past, not a single moment: *Nowadays people rarely write letters*, but *She's in the shower now*, not *She's in the shower nowadays*. In everyday American speech *these days* is more common.

senses.gloss: At the present time, compared with the past.
examples: *Nowadays*, almost everyone has a smartphone.
Hardly anyone pays by check *nowadays*.
Kids *nowadays* don't know what a cassette is.

position: mid — before the main verb, after *be*; also front
contrast: False friend: *actually* looks like Russian *актуально* / *актуальный*, but it means 'in fact' (*на самом деле*), never 'at the moment' or 'relevant'. 'At the moment' is *currently*: *She is currently working in Boston*; 'relevant, topical' is *relevant* or *current*.

senses.gloss: At the present time.
examples: She's *currently* working on her second novel.
The position is *currently* unfilled.
*Currently*, about forty people work at the plant.

position: mid — also before its word (*formerly known as*)
modifies: verbs, participles and names (*Myanmar, formerly Burma*)
contrast: *formerly* (in the past) and *formally* (officially, in a formal way) sound almost the same in American speech. For *бывший* before a noun, English uses the adjective *former* (*a former teacher*); *formerly* goes with a verb or a name.

senses.gloss: In the past, but not any longer.
examples: The restaurant was *formerly* a bank.
He *formerly* worked as a nurse in Ohio.
Myanmar, *formerly* known as Burma, is in Southeast Asia.

position: mid — also front, and after a time phrase (*two days previously*)
modifies: verbs, participles; follows a time phrase
contrast: *two years previously* (or *earlier*, *before*) counts back from a past point; counting back from now is *two years ago*. *previously* is formal — in speech, *before* or *earlier* is more natural.

senses.gloss: Before now or before the time mentioned, also after a time phrase (*three months previously*).
examples: She had *previously* worked for the city.
As *previously* mentioned, the office is closed on Monday.
He had left the company three months *previously*.

position: mid or end — mid for 'at one time in the past' (*I once lived there*); end for 'one time' (*I've been there once*)
contrast: Position changes the meaning: *I once lived in Ohio* (*когда-то*) against *I've been to Ohio once* (*один раз*). *at once* is 'immediately' or 'at the same time'; *all at once* is usually 'suddenly'. The conjunction *once* (*Once you start, you can't stop* = *как только*) belongs to another dictionary.

senses.gloss: One time; on one occasion.
examples: I've only been to New York *once*.
We meet *once* a week.
Take one pill *once* a day with food.

senses.gloss: At some time in the past, but no longer.
examples: This town was *once* a busy port.
I *once* met him at an airport in Dallas.
The house *once* belonged to a famous writer.

senses.gloss: Ever; even one time (after a negative).
examples: He never *once* said thank you.
Not *once* did she complain about the pain.

senses.gloss: Again; one more time (*once more*, *once again*).
examples: Let's try it *once more* from the top.
*Once again*, the team lost at home.

senses.gloss: Immediately (*at once*).
examples: Come here *at once*!
The doctor saw me *at once*.

senses.gloss: At the same time (*at once*).
examples: Don't all talk *at once*.
I can't do three things *at once*.

senses.gloss: Suddenly (*all at once*).
examples: *All at once*, the lights went out.
*All at once* she started laughing.

position: front or end
modifies: verbs and clauses, about the future
contrast: Future only: for the past use *one day* or *once* (*One day last spring, I met him*); *one day* works for both. *someday* is one word; *some day* is two when it means an unnamed particular day: *Let's have lunch some day next week*.

senses.gloss: At some unknown time in the future.
examples: I want to visit Japan *someday*.
*Someday* you'll understand why I did it.
Maybe *someday* we'll live by the ocean.

position: front — usually followed by a comma; also end
contrast: *meanwhile* is an adverb, not a conjunction: *I cooked; meanwhile, he set the table*, or *I cooked while he set the table* — not *I cooked meanwhile he set the table*. *in the meantime* can replace it for 'until then', but not for contrast.

senses.gloss: At the same time as something else is happening.
examples: I'll make the salad. *Meanwhile*, you can set the table.
The police searched the house; *meanwhile*, the suspect was already in Mexico.

senses.gloss: In the time before something expected happens.
examples: The new office opens in May. *Meanwhile*, we're working from home.
Your passport will take six weeks; *meanwhile*, don't book any flights.

senses.gloss: Used to contrast two situations.
senses.ru: между тем, в то же время
examples: Rents keep going up. *Meanwhile*, wages have barely moved.
The city spends millions on stadiums; *meanwhile*, schools are falling apart.

position: after its word — *three days ago*, never *ago three days*
modifies: a preceding time phrase (*two hours ago*, *long ago*, *a while ago*)
contrast: Past simple only: *I saw it two weeks ago*, not *I have seen it two weeks ago*. *ago* counts back from now; from a past point use *before*, *earlier* or *previously*: *She said she had met him two years before*. *ten years ago* answers 'when?' (*десять лет назад*); *for ten years* answers 'how long?' (*уже десять лет*).

senses.gloss: Back in time from now.
examples: She moved to Seattle three years *ago*.
How long *ago* did this happen?
I talked to him just a few minutes *ago*.

position: end
modifies: verbs; follows a time phrase (*the day before*)
contrast: As an adverb *before* stands alone at the end; the preposition (*before lunch*) and the conjunction (*before you go*) belong to other dictionaries. For 'ever in the past' use the present perfect: *Have we met before?* Counting back from now is *ago*: *three days ago*, not *three days before*. *the day before* is *накануне*.

senses.gloss: At an earlier time; in the past.
examples: Have we met *before*?
I've never seen anything like it *before*.
She had been to Paris twice *before*.

senses.gloss: After a time phrase: earlier than a past time.
examples: I'd seen him the week *before*.
The storm hit on Tuesday; the day *before*, the sky was perfectly clear.
He had left two hours *before*.

position: mid or end — end in *ever since*; mid in *has since been*, *long since*
modifies: verbs, usually in the present or past perfect
contrast: The preposition (*since Monday*) and the conjunction (*since I was ten*; *since* meaning 'because') belong to other dictionaries. With *since*, the verb goes in the perfect, unlike Russian: *I've known her since college*, not *I know her since college*. *since* marks the start, *for* the length: *for three years*, not *since three years*.

senses.gloss: From that time until now or until the time mentioned (often *ever since*).
examples: She moved to Denver in 2015 and has lived there ever *since*.
I saw him in May, but I haven't heard from him *since*.
They met at a party and have been friends ever *since*.

senses.gloss: At some time between then and now.
examples: The house has *since* been sold.
He left the band and has *since* started his own label.

senses.gloss: A long time before now (*long since*).
examples: The factory has long *since* closed.
Those old rules have long *since* been forgotten.

position: mid or end

senses.gloss: At once; with no delay at all.
examples: The driver was killed *instantly*.
I *instantly* regretted saying it.
Her voice is *instantly* recognizable.

position: mid — for 'now'; end or front for 'soon'
contrast: Two meanings that point in opposite directions. In American English *presently* most often means 'now' (*She is presently in Brazil*); the older 'soon' meaning (*I'll be with you presently*) is still met in fiction and formal speech. Mid position usually means 'now', end position usually means 'soon'.

senses.gloss: At the present time; now.
examples: The senator is *presently* on a trip overseas.
There are *presently* no plans to close the school.

senses.gloss: Soon; after a short time.
examples: The doctor will be with you *presently*.
*Presently* the door opened, and a young man came in.

position: front or end — front when ordering steps; mid in *when I next see…*; before its word in *next best*, *next to*
modifies: verbs; superlatives (*the next largest*); adjectives after *next to*
contrast: *next week*, *next year* use the determiner, with no *the* and no preposition: *See you next week*, not *on the next week*; *the next week* means 'the following week' from a past point. The preposition *next to* 'beside' (*Sit next to me*) belongs to another dictionary; before an adjective the adverb *next to* means 'almost'.

senses.gloss: Immediately after this or that; then.
examples: What should we do *next*?
*Next*, add the sugar and stir.
Guess who walked in *next*?

senses.gloss: On the first occasion after this one.
examples: When I *next* see him, I'll ask him about it.
When are you *next* in town?

senses.gloss: Following in order of size or rank (before a superlative).
examples: Texas is the *next* largest state after Alaska.
If you can't get the real thing, this is the *next* best option.

senses.gloss: Almost (*next to*, before an adjective or *nothing*).
examples: Finding parking downtown is *next* to impossible.
They sold the car for *next* to nothing.

position: mid or end — mid or front for 'at first'; end for 'by origin' (*Where are you from originally?*)
comparison: not gradable — except the rare 'creatively' sense (*more originally*)
contrast: False friend: Russian *оригинально* usually means 'unusually, creatively', but English *originally* almost always means 'at first' or 'by origin'. *The house was originally designed as a school* = *изначально*. For the Russian sense say *creatively*, *unusually* or *in an original way*.

senses.gloss: At first; before something changed.
examples: The building was *originally* a school.
*Originally*, we planned to drive, but we flew instead.
The song was *originally* recorded in 1965.

senses.gloss: As far as someone's or something's origin is concerned.
examples: Where are you from *originally*?
My family is *originally* from Ukraine.

senses.gloss: In a new and creative way.
examples: Few writers think as *originally* as she does.
Her dresses are simple but very *originally* designed.

position: mid — also front
contrast: *initially* and *at first* suggest that things changed later (*Initially I hated it, but…*); *first* and *firstly* put points or steps in order. *initially* is somewhat formal; in speech *at first* is more common.

senses.gloss: At the beginning, usually before a change.
examples: *Initially*, the project was supposed to take six months.
I was *initially* skeptical, but the plan worked.
The injury was worse than doctors *initially* thought.

position: any position — front for a dramatic turn (*Suddenly, …*), mid or end
contrast: Russian *а вдруг…?* ('what if') is not *suddenly*: *What if he doesn't come?*, not *And suddenly he doesn't come?*. *вдруг* in 'by chance' is *by any chance*: *Do you by any chance have a charger?*

senses.gloss: Quickly and unexpectedly.
examples: *Suddenly*, the lights went out.
He *suddenly* realized he'd left his wallet at home.
The weather changed *more suddenly* than anyone expected.

position: end
form: compound — *any* + *more*, written as one word in American English
contrast: Russian *уже не* / *больше не* is *not … anymore* or *no longer*: *He doesn't work here anymore* or *He no longer works here*, not *He already doesn't work here*. Standard English uses it only with a negative or in a question; the positive 'nowadays' use (*Anymore, gas is so expensive*) is regional Midland American speech and is best not copied. Two words, *any more*, is a quantity in both British and American English: *I don't want any more cake*.

senses.gloss: No longer; not now, as before (with a negative or in a question).
examples: We don't go to that restaurant *anymore*.
She doesn't live here *anymore*.
Does anyone even use fax machines *anymore*?

position: end — also front (*Earlier, …*) and after a time phrase (*two days earlier*)
comparison: not gradable — it is already the comparative of *early* (*much earlier*)
modifies: verbs; follows a time phrase (*an hour earlier*)
form: comparative of *early*, used as a time adverb in its own right
contrast: *two hours ago* counts back from now; *two hours earlier* counts back from a past point. For an earlier moment today, *earlier* is the natural word: *I called you earlier* (*я тебе сегодня уже звонил*); *before* alone sounds unfinished there.

senses.gloss: At a previous time, especially earlier today or in the same text or conversation.
examples: I saw your brother *earlier*.
As I mentioned *earlier*, the office is closed on Friday.
*Earlier* this year, the company opened a store in Miami.

senses.gloss: After a time phrase: before a past point.
examples: He had arrived two days *earlier*.
A week *earlier*, nobody had even heard of her.

senses.gloss: Sooner than another time or than usual.
examples: Can you come in *earlier* tomorrow?
I got up *earlier* than usual to beat the traffic.
